title: The butcher's last lesson
hookLine: inside the butcher's house, the last instruction sends the monk straight back home
carry: dharma begins with the family at your door
tomorrow: bhakti: Jayadeva's Gita Govinda, and the line he couldn't write

lines: A DOOR, A BIRD, A BUTCHER.
cards: A proud young monk burns a bird with a glare. A woman makes him wait at her door because she's caring for her husband. And a butcher in the market feeds his old parents before he will teach.
Day two hundred sixty-three stopped at his door. Vivekananda barely steps inside. The Mahabharata does.
And the butcher's last instruction is the one thing the monk never expected to hear.

teach.h: NO DUTY IS UGLY, NO DUTY IS IMPURE.
teach.b: Vivekananda gives one exchange from inside. The monk asks: with knowledge like yours, why are you in a butcher's body, doing such ugly work?
The butcher answers, in Vivekananda's telling, that no duty is ugly and no duty is impure.

The rest, Vivekananda says, is one of the highest flights of Vedanta, and the Mahabharata gives it in full: the Vyadha Gita, the song of the hunter. There the monk has a name, Kaushika, and the city is Mithila.
The butcher's trade came down to him in his family. He sells meat; he doesn't do the killing. Then he turns the monk's disgust around.

Nobody lives without harm; even the farmer's plow kills creatures in the soil. What a person can choose is the rest: telling the truth, holding back anger, giving, and caring for the people in their keeping.
He brings Kaushika in to meet his parents, and calls them his gods. Then he says the thing the monk least wants to hear.

teach.h: GO HOME TO YOUR OWN PARENTS.
teach.b: You left your own old father and mother, without their blessing, to go and study. They have grieved for you, the text says, until their eyes failed. Go home, and look after them.
That's your practice. The teacher sends the seeker straight back where he started.

teach.h: DHARMA BEGINS AT YOUR OWN DOOR.
teach.b: That's dharma as Hindus have long taught it: caring for the family in your keeping isn't a detour from the spiritual life.

It's why so many Hindu families bow to touch an elder's feet for a blessing, and why looking after aging parents counts as practice. Karma isn't only a grand mission far away. It's the duty waiting at your own door.

how: The story of the woman and the righteous butcher, the Vyadha Gita of the Mahabharata, is widely retold in Hindu homes and sermons, often through Vivekananda's version, to teach that one's own daily duties, done selflessly, are a spiritual path.

o: action, even the plain duty waiting at home
a vow to give up all work and live apart
a far-off mission that proves your worth

games.q: inside the butcher's house — tap the pairs.
p: the monk's name in the Mahabharata
the city where the butcher worked

s: the butcher asks Kaushika to stay and study with him for years
he sends him home to care for the parents he left behind.
the butcher says no one lives without harming something
even the farmer's plow kills creatures in the soil; what a person can choose is truth, restraint and care.
Vivekananda tells the butcher's whole teaching in his lecture
he gives one exchange and calls the rest one of the highest flights of Vedanta; the Mahabharata has it in full.

games.q: you're Kaushika. you traveled all the way to Mithila to learn from this butcher. he's taught you, and now he gives you one last instruction. what is it?
o: go home and look after your parents.
go back to the forest and meditate harder.
games.why: go home. the parents he left have grieved for him, and caring for them is his practice. the teacher sends the seeker back to where he started.

practice: Let one person come to mind whose care is partly yours: a parent, a child, a brother or sister, a friend who's been alone too long, someone close rather than someone you'd like to help someday, maybe someone you haven't called in a while.
See their face, and notice one small thing they might need from you, a call, a visit, a meal, no need to act on it now. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer.

wordCard.voice: Karma. Action. In the Vyadha Gita, a butcher teaches that no honest duty is impure, and sends a wandering monk home to his parents.

orig.note: Sanskrit: duty, what ought to be done, from kri, to do; the same root as karma.

carryVoice: Your line: dharma begins with the family at your door. The monk's long road ran back home. That's day three hundred fourteen.
